newsitem.title: CROATIA: Varazdinska says to grow into leading Croat bank.
newsitem.headline: Varazdinska says to grow into leading Croat bank.

text.p: Varazdinska Banka, one of three fully-listed Croatian firms, plans to quadruple its capital and grow from a regional into a leading national financial institution, a top bank official said on Thursday.
"Varazdinska Banka has to become one of the leading independent Croatian banks by 2002," chief executive Mato Lukinic told the bank's annual meeting.

Lukinic said the seven-year plan, created in cooperation with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), envisaged increasing the bank's capital to six billion kuna from the current 1.55 billion.
"This should enable the bank to support large investment projects and strengthen this region with cheaper capital, while also securing better results for shareholders," he said.
Representative of the EBRD, which acquired a 10 percent stake in the bank in October 1996, said it supported Varazdinska's ambitions to expand its base from the northern region to whole of Croatia.
"The EBRD considers the plan to be a very important challenge for the future," said Viktor Pastor, speaking on behalf of the European bank.
The EBRD's Dragica Pilipovic Chaffey, who sits on Varazdinska's supervisory board, said in the bank's newsletter:
"Our expectations are large. The bank should grow faster than it has grown so far."
Lukinic announced plans by Varazdinska to open two new branches in the coastal towns of Rijeka and Split, and a closed-type investment fund this year.
The bank, which has traditionally supported export businesses, was also considering mergers and acquisitions of other banks in the future to increase its competitiveness.
"By year 2002 Varazdinska plans to open representative offices in Frankfurt, Vienna and Milan," Lukinic said.
He described 1996 as "one of the most successful years" in the 40-year history of the bank, bringing it a strong increase in net profit to 28 million kuna.
The results were achieved through lowering the lending rate below the average in Croatia and cutting commission fees by almost 50 percent, Lukinic added.

Pastor saw room for future development in applying sound banking principles in lending and investment activity, development of new products in the retail market segment and increasing the level of productivity.
"All the previous points would lead toward reducing the financial costs for the bank's clients and increase its competiteveness," he said.
Varazdinska is 69-percent privatised and sees private ownership increasing to 80 percent this year as one of this major shareholders, textile firm Varteks, completes its own privatisation.
The share split of its stock, approved at the annual meeting, should also help the bank's further privatisation, said Pastor. All the shares will be reissued at 100 each.
Varazdinska's ordinary stock rose to 44,000 kuna on Thursday from 42,000 for the 16,000-kuna face value before the split.
